Summary

“Hey, Mydei.”

“Hm?”

“What’s the similarity between you and this garden?”

Mydei paused, suspicious. He straightened up and raised an eyebrow. “I don’t know. What?”

Phainon’s grin turned wicked. He stepped closer, voice dropping into a husky murmur.

“Because I’m gonna plow both of you thoroughly… and then plant my seeds real deep.”

Mydei stared at him for a second, stunned. Then he let out a loud, incredulous laugh, cheeks flushing despite himself.

“Oh my God,” he groaned, covering his face with one dirty glove. “That was terrible. Absolutely horrible.”

---

After burning out, Mydei retreats to a coastal village with no plan beyond silence. Until the local delivery man starts showing up more than necessary, who had way too many side hustles to count.

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Happy Accident
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

Playlist --> The Best Thing OST

The scooter tires screeched against the cracked coastal road, kicking up a small cloud of sand and dried pine needles.

Mydei jumped back just in time, heart pounding against his ribs. The delivery bag on the back of the scooter wobbled dangerously as the rider killed the engine and yanked off his helmet.

“Shit—! Are you okay?” The guy’s voice was rougher than expected, a little breathless. He swung a leg over the scooter and stepped closer, eyes wide with genuine panic. “I didn’t see you, the sun was right in my— fuck, I’m sorry.”

Mydei stood there clutching the paper bag of fresh bread and lemons he’d just bought from the tiny morning market, trying to steady his breathing. The coastal breeze tugged at his loose shirt, carrying the smell of salt and wild rosemary.

He looked at the delivery rider properly for the first time.

Tall. Messy hair with streaks of bleached silver that looked like they’d been done on a dare. Sun-browned skin, a faded scar across one eyebrow, and eyes the color of seawater. The name tag on his worn delivery jacket read Phainon.

“I’m… alive,” Mydei managed. His voice still sounded a little shaky. “Barely.”

Phainon let out a short, relieved laugh and rubbed the back of his neck. “Yeah, no thanks to me. I’ve been doing this route for three weeks and you’re the first person I’ve almost turned into roadkill. Congrats.”

Despite himself, Mydei’s mouth twitched. Him, the guy who had meticulously planned his burnout escape down to color-coded moving boxes, was now standing on the side of a dusty road getting apologized to by a delivery guy who looked like he belonged on the cover of a summer romance novel.

“You always drive like you’re being chased?” Mydei asked, raising an eyebrow.

“Whenever I’m late for the lunch rush at the harbor cafés, yes,” Phainon glanced at the bread bag in Mydei’s hand. “You new here? Haven’t seen you around.”

“Moved in two weeks ago. The little blue house past the olive grove.”

Phainon’s expression shifted into something like recognition. “Ah. The city guy. Mrs. Kallos mentioned someone quiet bought old man Theo’s place.” He smiled, crooked and unexpectedly charming. “Didn’t expect you to be cute, though.”

Mydei blinked.

Phainon seemed to realize what he’d said out loud and cleared his throat, suddenly very interested in the cracked asphalt. “I mean— welcome to the coast. Try not to get murdered by reckless delivery drivers.”

The wind picked up again, fluttering the edge of Phainon’s jacket and carrying the distant sound of waves crashing against the cliffs below.

Mydei adjusted his grip on the bread. His old city instincts told him to nod politely and walk away. His new, slower-life instincts (still very much under construction) told him something else.

“…You know the area better than I do,” Mydei said carefully. “If you almost kill me again, at least buy me coffee first. As compensation.”

Phainon looked up, surprise flashing across his face before it melted into a grin.

“Sure. I get off at seven. There’s a tiny place by the lighthouse that makes the best freddo espresso on this side of the peninsula.” He paused, then added, softer, “Name’s Phainon, by the way.”

“Mydei.”

“Nice to almost meet you, Mydei.”

Phainon climbed back onto the scooter, but before he put his helmet on, he glanced back one more time.

“Better walk on the sidewalk for the next few hours, yeah? I’d like that coffee date to actually happen.”

With a final cheeky salute, he revved the engine and drove off, leaving Mydei standing in the sunlight, heart still racing for entirely different reasons than burnout or near-death experiences.

---

Mydei pushed open the weathered wooden gate to his small blue house, the hinges creaking in the afternoon quiet. The paper bag of bread and lemons rustled against his leg as he stepped inside.

It still didn’t feel quite real. The walls were thick stone, cool even in the heat of the day, and the windows looked out over a gentle slope of wild thyme and olive trees down toward the sea. There was obviously no traffic, no neighbors shouting through thin apartment walls, and certainly no endless sound of the city that used to follow him even into sleep.

He set the bag on the kitchen counter and stood there for a long moment, listening to the silence. It pressed against his ears like something foreign. Comforting but strange. He kept waiting for the other shoe to drop, for the burnout to creep back in the absence of noise. Instead, his thoughts kept drifting back to those eyes and a crooked grin.

“Coffee,” he muttered to himself. “Just coffee. Don’t overthink it.”

He spent the next few hours trying to settle. Unpacking another box. Reading a few pages of a book he’d abandoned months ago. Taking a long shower with the window open so the sea air could drift in. By the time the sun had set, Mydei changed into a light linen shirt and walked down the winding path toward the lighthouse.

The tiny café sat on a bluff overlooking the water, its whitewashed walls glowing warmly in the evening light. A handful of wooden tables were scattered outside under a faded canvas awning. And there, leaning against the low stone wall with his hands in the pockets of a worn black hoodie, was Phainon.

He’d changed out of the delivery jacket. His hair was still messy, silver streaks catching the last of the sunlight. When he spotted Mydei approaching, his whole face lit up in that same easy, devastating smile.

“You actually came,” Phainon said, pushing off the wall. “I half-expected you to change your mind and barricade yourself behind all those city manners.”

“I considered it,” Mydei admitted, stopping a few steps away. The breeze tugged at his shirt. “But I figured I owed myself the chance to see if you’re a better driver when you’re not working.”

Phainon laughed. “Fair. Come on, best table’s still free.”

He led them to a small corner table right at the edge of the bluff. The sea stretched out below them, turning deep indigo as the sun sank. A young waitress brought over two glasses of freddo espresso topped with creamy foam, along with a small plate of loukoumades still warm from the fryer.

Phainon watched Mydei take his first sip, one eyebrow raised. “Verdict?”

“…Dangerously good,” Mydei said, surprised at how much he meant it. “I might have to rethink my whole ‘quiet life means no new addictions’ plan.”

Phainon’s grin widened. “That’s how this place gets you. One perfect coffee, one perfect sunset, and suddenly you’re selling your soul to the slow life.” He leaned back in his chair, studying Mydei openly. “So what’s your story, city boy? Most people who move out here are either running from something or looking for something. Which one are you?”

Mydei turned the cold glass in his hands, watching the foam swirl. The silence of his house echoed in his mind again.

“Both, maybe. I burned out pretty hard back home. High-pressure job, endless deadlines, exhaustion that makes you forget what your own voice sounds like.” He glanced up. “Figured if I didn’t leave, I’d break something I couldn’t fix. So… here I am. Learning how to sit with silence.”

Phainon nodded slowly, his expression softening.

“I get that,” he said after a moment. “I came out here a couple years ago too. Different reasons, but same feeling. The sea doesn’t care how loud your head is. It just keeps going. Helps, eventually.”

He reached over and nudged the plate of loukoumades closer to Mydei. Their fingers brushed for a second. Mydei felt that small touch travel up his arm like a spark.

Phainon cleared his throat, suddenly a little shy. “Anyway. I’m glad you showed up. Even if I did almost kill you this morning.”

Mydei smiled as the first stars began to appear over the water.

“Yeah,” he said softly. “Me too.”

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Benefits of Being Strangers
chapters.html:
Mydei took another sip of his freddo, the cold bitterness cutting through the sweetness of the foam. The conversation had flowed easier than he expected. Maybe it was the salt air, or the fact that Phainon was still half a stranger, someone with no expectations, no shared history, no silent judgment waiting in the wings.

“I didn’t realize how much I was performing back in the city,” Mydei said quietly. “Always ‘on.’ Always useful. The burnout didn’t even feel like burnout until I stopped moving. Now I wake up and the house is so quiet I can hear my own thoughts echoing. It’s terrifying sometimes. But also the first time in years I’ve felt like I might actually be myself again.”

Phainon listened without interrupting. He didn’t offer empty platitudes or try to fix it. He just nodded, turning his glass slowly between his fingers.

“Quiet can be a bastard,” he said eventually. “It shows you all the cracks you covered up with noise. But it’s honest, at least.” He gave a small, crooked smile. “You’re braver than most for choosing it on purpose.”

Mydei let out a soft breath he hadn’t realized he was holding. It was strange how freely the words came. He wouldn’t have said any of this to his old city friends. Not yet.

They talked longer than either expected. About the ridiculous number of olive trees around Mydei’s house, about Phainon’s worst delivery disasters, about the time Mydei once cried in a bathroom stall during a performance review. The sky had gone deep violet by the time the waitress quietly placed the bill on a small metal tray between them.

Phainon reached for it first, then paused. He rubbed the back of his neck, the easy confidence from earlier turning into something sheepish.

“Hey… mind if you cover mine?” he asked, voice lower than before. “My pay hits the account tomorrow. I’m good for it, I swear.”

Mydei blinked.

He had been reaching for his wallet already, but the request landed a little sideways. He shouldnʼt have agreed in the first place if he was short on money. But alas, it was him who had asked for compensation in the first place. But was it wrong? Heʼd almost gotten into accident, after all.

The rest of him noticed how Phainon’s ears had gone red under the silver streaks in his hair, and how he was suddenly very focused on a loose thread on his sleeve.

Mydei exhaled through his nose, then nodded.

“Sure,” he said, pulling out his card. “I’ve got it.”

Phainon’s shoulders relaxed visibly. “Thanks. Really. Next round’s on me. Promise.”

They stood up as the waitress took the payment. The night air had cooled, carrying the scent of the sea and pine. As they walked away from the café along the bluff path, the silence between them felt a little heavier than before.

Mydei glanced sideways at Phainon. “You could’ve said something earlier, you know.”

“I know.” Phainon shoved his hands into his hoodie pocket, kicking a small stone off the path. “Didn’t want you to think this was some broke-guy pity setup. I just wanted to talk to you. Without the whole almost-running-you-over thing hanging over it.”

Mydei slowed his steps. The irritation faded a little, replaced by something warmer.

“Next time,” Mydei said, testing the words, “maybe let the guy who just moved here and has disposable income buy the first round without the surprise twist.”

Phainon let out a short laugh, relief evident. “Really? So… there’s gonna be a next time?”

Mydei looked out at the lighthouse beam sweeping slowly across the water, then back at the man walking beside him.

“Yeah,” he said. “I think there is.”

The path back wound gently through stone walls and clusters of wild fennel. The lighthouse beam swept across the water in arcs, painting faint silver ripples on the sea. Their footsteps crunched softly on the gravel, a comfortable rhythm after the earlier awkwardness had eased.

Mydei kept his hands in his pockets, glancing sideways at Phainon. The question about money sat heavy on his tongue, but he didn’t want to make it blunt. Not after the guy had just opened up about the quiet and the cracks it revealed.

“So… delivery work,” Mydei started, keeping his tone light. “You’ve been doing it long? Seems like a pretty nonstop kind of job around here.”

Phainon gave a chuckle, catching the roundabout question easily enough. He didn’t seem offended. If anything, he looked a little relieved someone asked without pity in their voice.

“About eight months now,” he said, kicking another pebble ahead of them. “Before that I had a decent gig at the boatyard. Pay was okay. Life was steady.” He shrugged, the silver in his hair catching moonlight. “Then things went to shit. One bad investment after another, some debts I co-signed for a friend who disappeared, and suddenly I was bankrupt. Cleaned me out.” He said it plainly.

“I grew up with my grandmother,” Phainon continued after a moment. “She raised me after my parents, well, they weren’t around. She had this little house full of cats and lemon trees. We never had much, but it never felt poor, you know? Good food, lots of stories, someone always cheering for me. When I went bankrupt I had to sell the house to cover everything…”

Phainon exhaled through his nose, looking out toward the dark sea.

“It’s not a sob story. I’m young, I’m healthy, I’ve got two hands and this scooter, so I hustle. Double shifts, extra routes, whatever it takes. Some days it feels like I’m running just to stay in place.” He smiled, but it was quieter this time. “Doesn’t stop me from getting sad about it sometimes. Especially when I remember how things used to be.”

Mydei listened without interrupting, the gravel path curving uphill toward his blue house. The honesty hit him harder than expected.

“I’m sorry,” Mydei said eventually. “That sounds heavy to carry alone.”

Phainon waved it off gently. “It is what it is. I’m managing. And hey—” he bumped Mydei’s shoulder lightly with his own, “—at least I can almost run over interesting people on the job. Silver linings.”

They reached the gate of the little blue house. The outdoor lantern Mydei had left on glowed softly against the stone wall, moths fluttering around it. The silence of the countryside settled around them again, but this time it didn’t feel quite so foreign.

Mydei stopped at the gate and turned to face him.

“Thanks for tonight,” he said. “For the coffee and for talking. Even if you made me pay for it.”

Phainon grinned, the playful spark returning to his eyes. “Tomorrow’s payday. I’ll make it up to you. There’s a small night market down by the harbor on Sunday. My treat. For real this time.”

Mydei looked at him, then nodded.

“I’d like that,” he said.

Phainon lingered for a moment, like he wanted to say more, then gave a small nod. “Good. I’ll text you the details. Or… I’ll just show up and hope you don’t hide behind your lemon trees.”

With one last crooked smile, he turned and started walking back down the path, shoulders relaxed under the stars.

Mydei stayed by the gate a while longer, listening to the fading sound of footsteps and the endless murmur of the sea. The quiet inside his house didn’t feel empty when he finally stepped inside. It felt like it was waiting for something new.

---

Mydei woke the next morning, sunlight slipping through the half-open shutters in warm golden stripes across the wooden floor. Another morning without usual hums of city. Here, there were only distant seabirds and the rustle of breeze through the olive trees.

He padded into the kitchen, ground fresh beans, and made himself a simple pour-over. The rich aroma filled the small house as he carried the mug to the window overlooking the slope toward the sea. The weather was perfect: clear blue sky, gentle wind, which made staying indoors feel like a waste.

He sipped the coffee, letting the warmth settle in his chest. After a light breakfast of bread, tomatoes, olive oil, and a few slices of cheese, he pulled on comfortable shoes and stepped outside. The air smelled of wild herbs and salt. A proper stroll sounded right, maybe down toward the harbor, or along the coastal path he’d been meaning to explore.

He walked without a destination, letting his legs decide. The path eventually brought him into the small village center, where a few tavernas and cafés spilled tables onto the shaded square. One place in particular caught his eye— a modest family-run restaurant with blue-checked tablecloths and pots of blooming basil by the entrance. The smell of grilled octopus and fresh bread drifted out.

Mydei was considering whether to sit down for a cold drink when he saw him.

Phainon moved between tables, balancing a tray loaded with glasses and plates. He wore a simple white shirt with the sleeves rolled up and a black apron tied around his waist. His hair was slightly tamed today, though a few silver-streaked strands still fell across his forehead. When he turned and spotted Mydei standing near the entrance, his face broke into a surprised but genuinely pleased grin.

“Well, look who the sea dragged in,” Phainon called, setting the tray down at a table before walking over. A light sheen of sweat glistened on his neck from the morning rush. “Morning stroll, or are you stalking your almost-murderer?”

Mydei chuckled. “Morning stroll. Clearly the universe has a sense of humor.”

Phainon glanced back at his section. Only a few tables occupied this early. He wiped his hands on the apron and nodded toward an empty table tucked under a vine-covered pergola.

“Sit. I’ve got ten minutes before the next wave hits. House lemonade? It’s fresh, lots of mint.”

“Sure,” Mydei said, settling into the chair. “You work everywhere, huh?”

Phainon laughed softly as he disappeared inside and returned quickly with two tall glasses of pale yellow lemonade, condensation already beading on the sides. He dropped into the seat across from Mydei with a grateful sigh, stretching his legs under the table.

“Restaurant three days a week, deliveries the rest. Sometimes I help at the boatyard on weekends if they’re short.” He took a long drink, then met Mydei’s eyes with that same direct honesty from last night. “Payday did hit, by the way. So I don’t look completely pathetic.”

“You didn’t look pathetic,” Mydei said quietly. “Just human.”

Phainon’s expression softened. For a moment the busy server facade slipped, revealing the man who had talked about his grandmother and lemon trees under the stars.

“Thanks for that.” He tapped his glass against Mydei’s. “You sleeping any better in the quiet house?”

“A little. Still wake up expecting traffic noise.” Mydei glanced around the sunlit square, then back at Phainon. “Didn’t expect to see you in waiter mode today.”

“Life’s full of surprises,” Phainon replied, flashing that grin again. “Good ones, sometimes.” He checked his watch and stood reluctantly, picking up his tray. “I get off at four. If you’re still around the village later, or if you feel like company at your place…”

He left the invitation hanging, hopeful but not pushy.

Mydei felt a small, warm flutter in his chest, a feeling he hadn’t experienced in a very long time.

“I’ll be around,” he said.

Phainon’s smile widened as he backed toward the kitchen. “Good. Try the fried calamari if you stay for lunch. I’ll make sure it’s hot.”

He disappeared inside, but not before throwing one last look over his shoulder.

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Local Heartthrob
chapters.html:
Mydei stayed at the table under the vine-covered pergola longer than he originally planned. He ordered the fried calamari Phainon had recommended, and nursed another glass of cold lemonade while the morning slowly turned into a busier lunch hour.

He couldn’t help but watch Phainon.

The man moved between the tables. Balancing heavy trays, remembering orders without writing them down, flashing that crooked smile at tourists and locals alike even when sweat dampened the front of his white shirt. He joked with an elderly couple at one table, helped a child pick up a dropped toy at another, and still found time to refill water glasses.

Mydei felt something tighten in his chest as he observed him.

He’s carrying so much, he thought. Grandmother, debts, multiple jobs… and still smiling like that.

It stirred an uncomfortable mirror in his own mind. Mydei had left the city with enough savings to last a while but “a while” wasn’t forever. He had told himself he’d take six months, maybe a year, to truly rest and heal. But watching Phainon work reminded him that peace without purpose could easily turn stagnant.

He leaned back in his chair, absently turning the glass in his hands. The burnout had hollowed him out so completely that the idea of working again had felt terrifying. Yet here, in this slower place, maybe it didn’t have to be the same soul-crushing grind. Maybe something smaller, something that still left room for quiet mornings and walks by the sea.

By the time Phainon had a brief lull and swung by his table again, wiping his hands on his apron, Mydei had already started mentally listing possibilities. He could do remote freelance work that could be local and part-time, teaching, helping with tourist services… anything that wouldn’t drag him back into the fire he’d barely escaped.

“You good?” Phainon asked, voice slightly hoarse from the rush. His eyes lingered on Mydei’s face a second longer than necessary. “Calamari didn’t disappoint, right?”

“It was excellent,” Mydei replied honestly. “You were right.” He hesitated, then added, “You’re really good at this. All of it. I’ve been watching you run around and… it made me think.”

Phainon raised an eyebrow, leaning one hip against the table. “Think about what? My natural charm and grace under pressure?”

Mydei smiled faintly. “That too. But mostly… I can’t hide in my house forever. Savings don’t last indefinitely. Seeing you hustle like this… it’s motivating. In a slightly annoying way.”

Phainon’s expression softened with understanding. A tired but real smile tugged at his lips.

“Yeah. The sea doesn’t pay the bills,” he said quietly. “But it makes the hustling hurt less.” He glanced toward the kitchen where the owner was calling his name, then back to Mydei. “You don’t have to rush into anything brutal. There are slower jobs around here. People always need help with translations for tourists, or website stuff, or even guiding quiet walks for burnt-out city people.” His grin returned, playful again. “I could put in a good word if you want. Or just keep feeding you calamari while you figure it out.”

Mydei felt warmth spread through him that had nothing to do with the midday sun.

“I might take you up on that,” he said.

Phainon straightened as another table waved him over. “Four o’clock, remember? I’m off then.”

“I’ll be around,” Mydei promised.

Phainon gave him one last lingering look before diving back into the lunch rush.

Mydei stayed a while longer, finishing his meal slowly. The peace he had come here for didn’t have to mean doing nothing. Maybe it just meant doing things differently.

---

Mydei paid for his meal and left a generous tip, then stepped back out into the afternoon. With time to kill until four, he wandered the village at an easy pace.

He strolled past the small harbor where fishing boats bobbed gently, their paint faded by salt and sun. He walked along the stone promenade, watching children chase pigeons and old men play backgammon under the shade of plane trees. The air carried the smell of grilled fish, wild oregano, and the ever-present sea. For once, the lack of a strict schedule didn’t make him anxious.

He bought a small bag of roasted chickpeas from a street vendor and sat for a while on a wall overlooking the water, thinking again about work.

By ten minutes to four, he found himself back near the restaurant, drawn to Phainon’s scooter parked in the narrow side alley. The same one that had nearly turned him into a headline. Mydei leaned against the sun-warmed wall beside it, studying the machine with a half-smile.

The scratches on the side. The slightly dented delivery box. The worn seat. It looked exactly like what it was: a hardworking vehicle that had seen better days. Memories of squealing tires and Phainon’s panicked face flashed through his mind.

He was still standing there, lost in thought, when Phainon emerged from the back door. His shoulders slightly slumped with fatigue. He’d changed out of the white shirt into a simple black t-shirt, apron gone, hair more tousled than ever. He was pulling out his keys when he spotted the figure by his scooter.

Phainon stopped mid-step.

For a second, pure surprise crossed his face, followed immediately by a bright, unguarded delight that made his whole expression light up.

“You waited,” he said, voice warm with disbelief. “I figured you’d get bored and head back home.”

Mydei turned, one hand resting lightly on the scooter’s handlebar. “I considered it. Then I remembered this thing almost killed me.” He patted the seat with mock seriousness. “Thought I should face my trauma head-on.”

Phainon let out a laugh and closed the distance between them. Up close, he smelled like sun-warmed skin, faint restaurant spices, and a hint of the citrus soap he must have used to wash up.

“Brave of you,” he teased. “Most people would’ve run the other way after the second encounter.” His eyes softened as he looked at Mydei. “I’m glad you didn’t.”

“....”

Phainon rubbed the back of his neck, suddenly a little shy.

“I’m wiped, but… I still owe you. Properly this time.” He nodded toward the scooter. “I was gonna ride down to the night market later anyway. It’s nothing fancy, but the grilled corn is killer and there’s usually live music. If you’re not sick of me yet…”

“I’m not sick of you,” Mydei said quietly. “And I’d like that.”

Phainon’s crooked grin returned, brighter than before. He swung a leg over the scooter and patted the seat behind him.

“Hop on then, city boy. I promise I drive slower when I’m not late for a shift.”

Mydei hesitated only a second before climbing on. The scooter dipped slightly under their combined weight. He placed his hands lightly on Phainon’s sides, feeling the warmth of him through the thin t-shirt.

Phainon glanced back over his shoulder, his eyes catching the light.

“Hold on tighter if you want,” he said softly. “I don’t bite.”

The engine revved to life, and they pulled out of the alley together. The coastal wind rushed past them as the village gave way to winding roads lined with olive trees and glimpses of glittering sea.

Mydei didn’t mind the slight thrill in his stomach. It didn’t feel like burnout anymore.

.
.
.

The scooter slowed as they reached the edge of the harbor square, where the night market had come alive under strings of warm fairy lights and paper lanterns swaying in the sea breeze. The air was thick with the scent of grilled corn, souvlaki, fresh herbs, and sweet loukoumades. Music drifted from the far end and a singer performing old folk songs that made people clap along.

Phainon killed the engine and helped steady the scooter as Mydei swung off. Even though Mydei had passed through this market once before on his first week here, he had only walked the edges then, still too wrapped up in his own thoughts to really see it.

Tonight felt entirely different. It was alive.

Vendors called out to each other, locals laughed in clusters, children ran between stalls with sticky hands, and the golden light made everything feel softer and warmer.

Before they’d even taken three steps, the greetings started.

“Phainon! Finally, you show your face!” an older woman selling handmade soaps and olive oil candles waved enthusiastically. “Tell your grandmother I have that lavender salve she likes.”

A fishmonger with a thick mustache grinned from behind his ice-filled stall. “Eh, delivery boy! You still owe me a rematch at tavli.”

Two young women at a jewelry stand giggled and called out, “Phainon, who’s the new friend?” while a group of older men playing cards under a plane tree lifted their glasses in greeting.

Phainon returned every greeting with his signature smile — waving, exchanging quick words, promising to stop by later. He seemed to know half the market by name.

Mydei walked beside him, watching the whole thing unfold with raised eyebrows. Eventually, he leaned in close enough that his shoulder brushed Phainon’s.

“So… local celebrity, huh?” he teased. “Should I be asking for an autograph? Or do you charge extra for photos with fans?”

Phainon let out a surprised laugh, cheeks coloring just slightly under the lantern light.

“Shut up,” he muttered, bumping Mydei’s shoulder back. “It’s not like that. I’ve been delivering to most of these people for months. You show up with someone’s fresh bread or medicine when they need it and suddenly everyone acts like you’re their favorite nephew.”

“Mm-hmm,” Mydei hummed, unconvinced. “Sure. That’s why the soap lady lit up like she saw a movie star and those girls at the jewelry stall were blatantly checking you out.”

Phainon rubbed the back of his neck, visibly embarrassed now. “They’re just friendly. This is a small place. Everyone knows everyone.”

“Except the new city boy who almost got flattened by the local heartthrob on a scooter,” Mydei added, smirking.

Phainon stopped walking and turned to him fully, eyes sparkling with amusement.

“Heartthrob?” he echoed, stepping a little closer. “Keep talking like that and I might start thinking you like me, Mydei.”

The teasing died on Mydei’s tongue for a second. Up close, with the golden lights catching the silver in Phainon’s hair and the faint scent of his skin mixed with the market smells, it was hard to keep his voice steady.

“Then keep thinking like that,” Mydei said quietly, surprising even himself with how honest it came out.

Phainon’s expression softened, the playful grin fading into something almost like wondering. For a moment, the noise of the market seemed to fade into the background.

Then Phainon cleared his throat and nodded toward a stall ahead. “Come on. Let me fulfill my promise. Best grilled corn in the peninsula. And this time I’m paying.”

They continued walking side by side through the cheerful crowd. Mydei felt lighter than he had in months. The quiet life he’d been searching for suddenly felt a lot less quiet, and a lot more interesting.

And Phainon kept glancing at him with that same delighted look he’d worn earlier when he realized Mydei had waited for him, like he couldn’t quite believe this was happening either.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Most Employed Man
chapters.html:
They wandered the market a little longer, collecting food as they went. True to his word, Phainon bought two ears of grilled corn slathered in butter, paprika, and lemon. They also picked up a shared portion of fried zucchini balls, a small bag of warm pita with smoky eggplant dip, and two cold bottles of orange soda.

With their hands full, Phainon led them away from the lively heart of the market, down a short flight of stone steps to a quiet spot overlooking the water. It was a wide, flat rock formation just past the pier, close enough to hear the soft music and laughter drifting from the square, but far enough to feel private. The sea stretched dark and calm below them, reflecting scattered lights like scattered stars.

They sat side by side, legs dangling over the edge. The rock still held some of the day’s warmth.

Phainon handed Mydei one of the corn cobs and grinned. “As promised. Payment for the coffee I couldn’t afford yesterday.”

Mydei took a bite. The corn was sweet, smoky, and perfectly charred. “This is so good,” he murmured. “I might forgive you completely.”

They ate in comfortable silence for a few minutes, enjoying the food and the sound of gentle waves lapping against the rocks below.

Eventually, Mydei wiped his fingers on a napkin and glanced over at Phainon. “So, how was your day? You were moving nonstop when I was there. Looked exhausting.”

Phainon shrugged, chewing thoughtfully before answering. “Busy, but not bad. Saturday lunch rush is always brutal. Two big families from Athens showed up and ordered half the menu. I dropped two glasses like an idiot, but the owner didn’t chew me out too hard.” He gave a tired but genuine smile. “Tips were decent though. Makes the sore feet worth it.”

He took another bite of corn, then added more quietly, “Days like today remind me why I do the multiple jobs thing. Feels good to be moving around, even when I’m dead tired by the end.”

Mydei nodded, watching the way the lantern light played across Phainon’s face. After a moment, he spoke again, voice a little hesitant.

“I’ve been thinking about that too,” he admitted. “Watching you today… it hit me that I’ve been doing almost nothing for weeks now. At first it was perfect. Exactly what I needed after the burnout. But lately the days feel too empty. I wake up, make coffee, stare at the sea, go for walks, read a bit. Then repeat. I’m starting to get bored of having no routine at all.”

He picked at the edge of the pita bread, glancing sideways at Phainon.

“I don’t want to go back to the old life, but I think I might need something. Even if it’s small. Part-time. Something that gives me a reason to leave the house and feel useful again.”

Phainon listened quietly. He set down his half-eaten corn and turned more fully toward Mydei.

“You’re not rushing it?” he asked gently. “A lot of people come here and crash hard because they try to fill the quiet too fast.”

“I’m not rushing,” Mydei said. “But I’m also not sure I want to spend another month just floating. It’s starting to feel more like hiding than healing.”

Phainon was quiet for a moment, then gave a small, understanding nod.

“There are options around here,” he said. “The tourism office sometimes needs English speakers for guiding or admin stuff. Old Mrs. Liras runs a small guesthouse and always complains she needs help with bookings. Or you could do freelance work from your house. No one has to know how many hours you actually work.”

He bumped Mydei’s knee lightly with his own. “And if you want, I can ask around for you.”

Mydei felt a warm flutter in his chest at the casual offer of support.

“I’d like that,” he said softly. “Thank you.”

Phainon gave a boyish smile that made the silver in his hair look even brighter under the lights. He leaned back on his hands, shoulder brushing Mydei’s.

“Anytime,” he murmured. “We burnt-out hustlers gotta stick together.”

They stayed there long after the food was gone, talking quietly as the market music played faintly in the background and the sea kept its rhythm below.

---

A few days later, Mydei was sitting on the small terrace of his blue house with a book he wasn’t really reading when he heard the sound of a scooter coming up the dirt path.

He glanced up, expecting perhaps a neighbor or the postman. Instead, the same worn delivery scooter he knew too well rolled to a stop by his gate. The rider pulled off his helmet, revealing messy silver-streaked hair and a crooked grin.

Phainon.

Mydei stood up, eyebrows raised in genuine surprise. “You again? What happened to the restaurant this time?”

Phainon laughed as he unstrapped a medium-sized cardboard box from the back of the scooter. He was wearing a different vest today of a courier company logo printed on the back.

“Parcel for Mydei,” he announced in an official tone, then immediately dropped it. “Special delivery from your favorite local heartthrob.”

Mydei walked over to the gate, a smile tugging at his lips. “I thought you already had too many jobs. Now you’re delivering parcels too?”

Phainon handed him the box and leaned against the scooter, wiping sweat from his forehead with the back of his hand.

“Yeah, I started this week. The courier company needed extra hands for the coastal route. I know pretty much every address within twenty kilometers because of the food deliveries, so they hired me on the spot. Hours are super flexible — I can do mornings or evenings around the other shifts.” He shrugged, though there was a hint of tiredness in his eyes. “Money’s decent, thatʼs that.”

Mydei turned the parcel in his hands. It was the new coffee grinder he’d ordered online during one of his restless mornings. He looked back at Phainon.

“You’re going to burn yourself out at this rate,” he said, quieter this time. There was concern in his voice.

Phainon gave a lopsided smile and rubbed the back of his neck.

“I know. But grandmotherʼs apartment rent went up last month, and I still have some debts to clear. This job fits perfectly between the others. I can work when I need to and rest when I don’t.” He met Mydei’s gaze. “Plus, I get to show up at cute city boys’ houses with packages sometimes. Nice bonus.”

Mydei felt his ears warm. He set the box down on the low stone wall and stepped a little closer.

“Still. You don’t have to do everything alone, you know.”

Phainon looked at him. The playful mask slipped just a little.

“I’m not used to hearing that,” he admitted. Then he straightened up and tapped the parcel lightly. “Anyway, sign here so I can officially say I delivered it.”

Mydei signed on the little device, then hesitated before asking, “Do you have time for a drink? I just made fresh lemonade.”

Phainon checked the time on his phone, then smiled.

“I’ve got a few minutes before the next drop-off. Lemonade sounds perfect.”

They sat together on the terrace, the sea sparkling in the distance. Phainon stretched his legs out with a tired sigh while Mydei brought out two glasses. The quiet between them felt easy now, familiar.

“You know,” Mydei said after a while, watching Phainon’s relaxed posture, “watching you juggle all these jobs, it’s making me more sure I need to find something too.”

Phainon turned to him, eyes warm. “Youʼll find one soon.”

He reached over and lightly bumped his glass against Mydei’s.

---

After Phainon finished his lemonade, he took off to deliver the rest of the parcels. Mydei opened his laptop with a new sense of purpose. He spent the better part of two hours updating his resume, trimming the corporate jargon, highlighting relevant skills, and trying to make his high-pressure city background sound like an asset rather than a warning sign.

He printed a few copies, put on a neat but casual shirt, and headed into the village.

There weren’t many job postings online for the area. A couple of cafés needed part-time help, a small guesthouse wanted someone for reception and bookings, and one souvenir shop was looking for extra hands during the upcoming tourist season. Mydei decided the best approach was simply walking in.

The first few attempts seemed promising.

At the guesthouse, the owner seemed impressed by his experience. But when she asked about his long-term plans and he admitted he had moved here for a slower life, her smile faltered. “We need someone who will stay at least a year,” she said gently. “Not someone still figuring things out.”

The waterfront café was even quicker. The manager glanced at his resume, raised his eyebrows at the previous salary level, and said, “You’re overqualified. We need someone who won’t get bored and leave in two months.”

Small souvenir shop. Bookstore. Even a local minimarket.

Rejection after polite rejection.

By late afternoon, Mydei was walking back toward his blue house with a stack of untouched resumes in his bag and a heavy feeling in his chest. He replayed every conversation in his head.

Did I sound too eager? Too detached? Did I talk too much about the city? Or not enough about wanting to stay?

He sat on the wall outside his gate, staring at the sea without really seeing it. The quiet he had once craved now felt mocking.

“What am I doing wrong?” he muttered to himself. His resume was strong — excellent references, solid experience, and multilingual. And yet every small business owner seemed to sense something in him that made them hesitant. Maybe they could sense the burnout on him. Maybe they thought he was just another city escapist who would run back at the first sign of difficulty.

The sun was beginning to dip when he heard a familiar sound of a scooter approaching. Phainon pulled up, still wearing his courier vest, helmet tucked under his arm. His smile faded the moment he saw Mydei’s expression.

“Hey… rough day?” Phainon asked, killing the engine and walking over.

Mydei let out a tired breath and gave a weak smile. “I decided to start looking for work. Walked into a bunch of places. Got turned down by all of them.” He gestured at the folder beside him. “Apparently I’m either overqualified or suspiciously under-committed. Or both.”

Phainon sat down on the wall next to him. He stayed quiet for a moment, just listening.

“It’s not you,” he said eventually. “Not really. Small places here are careful. They’ve had too many people come for the ‘dream life,’ work two weeks, then disappear when they realize it’s actually quiet and the pay is modest.” He bumped Mydei’s knee gently. “They don’t know yet that you’re different.”

Mydei laughed without much humor. “I’m starting to wonder if I even know that.”

Phainon turned to look at him properly.

“You’re still adjusting. That takes time. And it’s okay if today sucked.” He reached over and lightly squeezed Mydei’s shoulder. “Want me to ask around more discreetly? Or we can just sit here and complain about capitalism while the sun sets. Both options are valid.”

Mydei leaned into the touch without thinking. The warmth of Phainon’s hand, the familiar scent of sun and sea eased something tight in his chest.

“Maybe both,” he said quietly. “In that order.”

Phainon smiled. “Nice. And for what it’s worth, I’m glad you’re here. Even if the local shops are too blind to see how lucky they’d be to have you.”

They stayed on the wall as the sky turned orange and pink, the quiet no longer feeling quite so heavy with Phainon beside him.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Iʼm Proud Of You
chapters.html:
The next day, Mydei woke with a mix of determination and lingering doubt. He made his coffee, printed fresh copies of his resume, and headed back into the village. He refused to let yesterday’s rejections keep him inside his house.

He tried two more places in the morning, but met with the same polite but firm rejections. “We need someone more local,” or “We’re really looking for someone who can work full days.” Each one stung a little less than the day before, but the weight was still there.

Just as he was considering calling it quits for the day, he stepped into a modest bookstore and stationery shop tucked near the edge of the square. The owner, a middle-aged man named Mr. Kostas with reading glasses perched on his head, was sorting through a box of new arrivals behind the counter.

Mydei introduced himself and explained he was looking for part-time work. The man glanced at the resume, raised his eyebrows at Mydei’s corporate background, and then paused.

“You speak English fluently?” he asked.

“Native level. I used to work with international clients.”

Mr. Kostas set the resume down and studied him for a moment. “My son is fourteen. He’s going to high school in the city next year and his English is… not great. He needs help if he wants to keep up. I can’t pay much, but it would be three afternoons a week, maybe four. Here in the back room or at our house. Would you be interested in tutoring him?”

Mydei blinked, surprised. It wasn’t what he had imagined, but something about it felt right. It was flexible, meaningful, and far removed from the soul-crushing office life he’d escaped.

“I’d be happy to,” he said. “I don’t have formal teaching experience, but I’m good with languages and explaining things clearly.”

They talked for another ten minutes. Mr. Kostas seemed relieved to find someone patient and competent. Mydei asked if he could start this weekend for an introductory session, and the owner readily agreed.

When he left the shop, the afternoon sun felt warmer on his skin.

---

Later that evening, as the sky was turning soft gold, Mydei found Phainon near the harbor. He was finishing a delivery run, locking up his scooter when Mydei approached.

Phainon turned and immediately noticed the brighter look on Mydei’s face.

“You look like you have news,” he said, wiping his hands on his jeans. “Good news?”

Mydei couldn’t stop the smile from spreading.

“I got a job. Sort of. I’m going to be an English tutor for Mr. Kostas’s son — the guy who owns the bookstore. Three or four afternoons a week. I start this weekend.”

Phainon’s entire face lit up. He stepped forward and pulled Mydei into a quick, enthusiastic hug, smelling like sun and sea air.

“That’s amazing!” he laughed, pulling back but keeping his hands on Mydei’s shoulders. “See? I told you they’d be lucky to have you. A tutor… that suits you way better than stacking shelves or serving tables.”

Mydei felt warmth bloom in his chest at Phainon’s genuine excitement.

“It’s not much, but it’s still work. Flexible hours, and I get to use my skills without going back to that old pressure cooker life.” He shrugged, a little shy. “I’m nervous about teaching a teenager, though.”

“You’ll be great,” Phainon said confidently. “You’re patient. You listen. And you already survived talking to me when I almost ran you over — a fourteen-year-old should be easy after that.”

They started walking slowly along the promenade together, the sea glittering beside them.

“I’m proud of you,” Phainon added more quietly, bumping their shoulders. “For trying again even after yesterday sucked.”

Mydei glanced at him, heart feeling strangely full.

“Thanks. I couldn’t have kept going without your encouragement the other day.”

Phainon’s ears turned a little pink. He looked out at the water for a moment before turning back with that familiar crooked smile.

“So, when you’re not busy turning Kostas’s kid into a future scholar, maybe we can celebrate? I still owe you a proper dinner.”

Mydei smiled.

“I’d like that.”

The two of them walked side by side as the first stars appeared.

---

Saturday afternoon arrived warm and golden. Mydei arrived at Mr. Kostas’s home above the stationery shop right on time, carrying a notebook and a couple of simple English books he thought might be useful. Mr. Kostas greeted him warmly and led him upstairs to a small, tidy living room that overlooked the harbor.

“This is my son, Caelus,” Mr. Kostas said, gesturing to the boy slouched on the couch.

Caelus was fourteen, all messy gray hair, oversized hoodie, and earbuds still half-in despite his father’s presence. He barely looked up from his phone when they entered, offering only a lazy “Hey” in response to the introduction.

“Nice to meet you, Caelus,” Mydei said calmly, keeping his voice even and friendly. He’d expected this. He remembered being fifteen and hating anything like extra schoolwork.

Mr. Kostas gave his son a pointed look, then excused himself to let them work. The moment the door clicked shut, Caelus let out a long, dramatic sigh and finally glanced at Mydei.

“So you’re the city guy who’s supposed to fix my English,” he muttered, tone dripping with teenage indifference. “I don’t even know why I need this. I can speak fine.”

Mydei sat down across from him at the small table, unfazed. He remembered that exact defensive posture. It was the armor of someone who felt like the world was forcing him into something he didn’t want.

“You probably can speak fine,” Mydei replied honestly. “But your dad mentioned you’re heading to high school in the city next year. The expectations there are different. I’m not here to make you sound like a textbook. I just want to make sure you don’t get eaten alive by assignments and exams.”

Caelus eyed him suspiciously, but at least he put his phone down.

Mydei continued, keeping his tone light. “Look, I was a grumpy teenager once too. I hated extra lessons. So I’m not going to force you to love English. We’ll just work on whatʼs only important so you can do well without suffering too much. Sound fair?”

There was a long pause. Caelus shrugged, but the hostility in his shoulders eased just a fraction.

“…Whatever.”

They spent the next hour going over the lessons. Mydei asked about Caelus’s current level, what he struggled with most, and what topics actually interested him. Instead of starting with dry grammar, Mydei sketched out a loose plan.

By the end of the hour, Caelus wasn’t exactly enthusiastic, but he was at least answering in full sentences and had stopped giving one-word replies.

“Not terrible, I guess,” Caelus mumbled as they wrapped up.

Mydei smiled. “High praise. See you on Tuesday?”

“Yeah… sure.”

---

As Mydei walked back down toward the harbor, the sun was just beginning to set. He felt a quiet sense of accomplishment.

He spotted Phainon waiting near the stone steps where they’d eaten grilled corn that night. The moment Phainon saw him, his face lit up with a boyish grin.

“How’d it go with the new student?” he asked, falling into step beside Mydei.

“Typical edgy teenager. Zero enthusiasm at first,” Mydei chuckled. “But I think we’ll be okay. He’s a good kid under all the brooding.”

Phainon bumped their shoulders together. “Told you you’d be good at this. Want to celebrate with dinner at my place tonight? It’s small and messy, but I make a mean pasta.”

Mydei glanced at him.

“I donʼt refuse free food.”

Phainon’s smile softened, eyes catching the sunset colors.

---

Phainon’s place was tucked behind a row of old stone houses, just a short walk uphill from the harbor. It was smaller than Mydei had imagined, basically a converted studio above a storage garage.

The living area and kitchen were one open space with wooden beams across the ceiling. Warm lamplight bathed the room in an equally warm glow. There were books stacked on almost every surface, a few potted herbs on the windowsill, and a worn but comfortable-looking couch covered with a colorful throw blanket. Photos of an older woman and younger Phainon smiled from a small shelf.

It reminded Mydei so strongly of his grandparents’ old house from childhood visits that he had to pause for a second in the doorway.

“Welcome to my humble kingdom,” Phainon said with a sheepish grin, rubbing the back of his neck. “It’s small, but it’s comfortable. Sit, I’ll handle dinner.”

“No way,” Mydei replied, already rolling up his sleeves. “You’ve been working all day. I’m not just going to sit and watch you cook like some guest.”

Phainon tried to protest. “Hey, I invited you. This is supposed to be my treat—”

“I’m helping,” Mydei said firmly, stepping into the tiny kitchen area. “I feel weird just standing there while you do everything. Let me chop something at least.”

Phainon looked at him for a moment, then laughed softly, the sound warm and fond. “Stubborn city boy. Fine. You can chop the tomatoes and onions. Donʼt cut your fingers off or I’d feel personally responsible.”

They worked side by side in the cramped space. Phainon stirred pasta and a simple tomato sauce on the stove while Mydei handled the vegetables. The radio played in the background, some old Greek folk song mixed with gentle waves of bouzouki. Every time Mydei reached for something, Phainon seemed to anticipate it, handing him a knife or a bowl without needing to be asked.

“You know,” Mydei said quietly as he diced tomatoes, “this place feels… nice. It reminds me of my grandmother’s house when I was little.”

Phainon glanced over, his expression softening. “Yeah? It’s nothing fancy, but it works. After I lost grandmaʼs old house, I told myself I’d rather have something small than nothing at all.” He bumped Mydei’s hip lightly with his own. “Plus, the view from the window isn’t bad.”

Mydei looked up. Through the open window, he could see the dark sea glittering under the rising moon and scattered lights from the village below.

“It’s perfect,” he murmured.

Phainon was quiet for a moment, then spoke without looking away from the pan. “You’re the first person I’ve invited over in a long time. Usually I just meet people at the market or café.”

Mydei felt a flutter in his stomach. He set the knife down and turned slightly toward Phainon.

“I’m glad you invited me.”

Their eyes met. For a moment, the only sounds were the gentle bubbling of sauce and the soft music. Phainon’s gaze dropped briefly to Mydei’s lips before he cleared his throat and turned back to the stove, ears slightly pink.

“Dinner’s almost ready,” he said, voice a little rougher than before. “Hope you’re not expecting fine dining.”

Mydei smiled, leaning against the counter. “I’m expecting good company. The food is just a bonus.”

Phainon let out a soft laugh and nudged a plate of grated cheese toward him.

“Okay then, you might not wanna leave after this.”

“Haha. Weʼll see about that.”

Mydei’s heart beat a little faster as the cozy little apartment seemed to shrink around them in the warm light.

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Perfect Middle Ground
chapters.html:
They carried the plates to the small wooden table by the window. Spaghetti with a rich tomato-basil sauce, grilled sardines with lemon, and a fresh salad drizzled with olive oil. A half-bottle of local red wine sat between them.

For a while, they ate comfortably, the clink of utensils and the sound of waves through the open window filling the space. Then Phainon started talking.

And once he started, he didn’t really stop.

He told Mydei about the funniest delivery disasters he’d had. There was a time a goat had chased him down a hillside. He talked about his grandmother’s stubbornness to stop gardening even in her small apartment balcony, and how she still scolded him for working too hard. He spoke about the village gossip, the upcoming summer festival, the hidden cove only locals knew about where the water was exaggeratedly clear.

Phainon’s voice was warm and animated, hands moving expressively as he spoke. Every so often he’d laugh at his own stories that made Mydei’s chest feel strangely full.

Mydei barely said anything. He just listened, nodding, smiling at the right moments, occasionally asking a small question to keep Phainon going. For once, he didn’t feel the need to fill the silence or perform. He was perfectly content to let Phainon’s voice wrap around him. After months of noisy city life and then overwhelming quiet, listening to Phainon talk felt like the perfect middle ground.

Phainon eventually noticed, pausing mid-story with a sheepish grin.

“I’m talking your ear off, aren’t I? You’ve barely said ten words since we sat down.”

Mydei shook his head, swallowing his last bite of pasta.

“I like listening to you,” he said simply. “Keep going.”

Phainon stared at him for a second. Then he smiled shyly and continued talking, though his voice had gentled.

They finished the wine and the meal slowly. The night grew darker outside, the moon climbing higher over the sea.

Eventually, Mydei helped clear the table despite Phainon’s half-hearted protests. When it was time to leave, they stepped out into the cool night air together.

Phainon walked him down the short path to the main road.

“Thanks for coming over,” he said quietly. “And for helping with dinner. And… for listening to me ramble for two hours straight.”

Mydei turned to face him under the soft glow of a streetlamp. “I meant it. I enjoyed tonight. A lot.”

They stood closer than necessary. Phainon’s eyes searched Mydei’s face like he was waiting for permission for something.

Then he leaned in and pressed a gentle, lingering kiss to Mydei’s cheek.

“Goodnight, city boy,” he murmured. “Get home safe.”

Mydei’s skin tingled where Phainon’s lips had touched.

“Goodnight,” he replied softly.

Phainon stayed at the edge of the path, watching until Mydei disappeared around the bend toward his blue house. The walk home felt lighter, the quiet night filled with the memory of warm lamplight, good food, and Phainon’s voice.

---

That night, after returning to his little blue house, Mydei couldn’t stop replaying the evening.

He lay in bed, staring at the ceiling beams, the taste of red wine and tomato sauce still lingering on his tongue. Phainon’s laugh, the way his eyes had softened when Mydei said he liked listening to him, and the gentle kiss on his cheek — all played on repeat.

It’s too soon, Mydei thought. They were still getting to know each other. Still dancing around whatever this was. But it was undeniable now. There was something between them. A pull. A thing.

He fell asleep with that thought, a small smile still tugging at his lips.

---

The next morning, Mydei woke up lighter than usual. He made coffee the same way he always did, yet caught himself humming while grinding the beans. When he watered the herbs on his windowsill, he realized he was smiling for no particular reason. Even while folding laundry, the corners of his mouth kept lifting.

He shook his head at his own reflection in the mirror.

“Pathetic,” he muttered, but the smile stayed.

By noon, his fridge looked embarrassingly empty. He grabbed a reusable bag and headed out toward the village market to refresh his stocks.

The sun was bright and warm as he walked the coastal path. He was still thinking about what to cook for the week when he passed a small community garden plot nestled between two old houses. Someone was bent over a row of tomato plants, pulling weeds.

Mydei slowed down.

It was Phainon.

He was wearing an old white t-shirt that had clearly seen better days. The thin fabric was damp with sweat, clinging to the lines of his back and shoulders as he worked under the sun. His arms were tanned and toned from months of physical jobs, and the shirt had ridden up slightly, revealing a strip of skin at his lower back. His messy hair was even more disheveled than usual.

Phainon straightened up, wiping sweat from his forehead with the back of his wrist. When he spotted Mydei standing on the path, his entire face lit up with his signature crooked smile.

“Well, if it isn’t my favorite city boy,” he called out, tossing a handful of weeds into a bucket. “Out exploring or running away from your own good mood?”

Mydei walked closer, trying to keep his eyes from drifting over the way the damp t-shirt outlined Phainon’s chest.

“Restocking the kitchen,” Mydei answered, smiling despite himself. “Didn’t expect to find you playing gardener.”

Phainon glanced down at himself and let out a short laugh. “One of the old ladies who owns this plot asked for help. Figured I’d do it before my shift starts. Free vegetables in return.” He stretched his arms above his head, the movement pulling the shirt even tighter against his body. “You okay? You’ve got this weird look on your face.”

Mydei cleared his throat, ears warming. “Just… thinking. About last night.”

Phainon’s expression softened. He stepped closer to the wooden fence separating the garden from the path, close enough that Mydei could smell sun-warmed skin and fresh earth.

“Yeah?” he asked, voice quieter. “Good thoughts, I hope.”

“Very good thoughts,” Mydei admitted.

Phainon’s gaze dropped to Mydei’s mouth for a brief second before he smiled again.

“I’ve got another hour here,” he said. “But if you’re free later, maybe we could take a walk? Or you could come over again. I still owe you for all the times you’ve fed me.”

Mydei didn’t even pretend to think about it.

“Free dinner,” he said. “Why not.”

Phainon’s grin returned, bright and hopeful under the morning sun. The white t-shirt stuck to him, the garden smelled of warm soil and basil, and Mydei realized he was smiling again.

The slow life was starting to feel a lot like falling.

---

Later that evening, Mydei found himself back at Phainon’s small apartment. The sun had already set, leaving the sky in soft shades of lavender and deep blue. Phainon had insisted on cooking again, this time using the fresh vegetables he’d earned from the garden.

The meal was much simpler than last night. A quick vegetable stir-fry with garlic and olive oil, some leftover pasta, and crusty bread. They moved around each other in the tiny kitchen, but unlike yesterday’s easy rhythm, the atmosphere felt heavy tonight. Every accidental brush of hands or arms made them both pause for half a second.

Phainon was quieter than usual. Mydei kept catching him stealing glances, only for Phainon to look away quickly and focus too intently on chopping vegetables.

The tension finally became too much for Mydei to ignore.

He set down the wooden spoon he was using to stir the pan and turned to face Phainon properly.

“Hey,” Mydei said softly. “Can we talk for a second?”

Phainon froze, then slowly put the knife down. He wiped his hands on a dish towel, looking a little nervous, which was oddly endearing on someone usually so confident and playful.

“Yeah. Of course.”

Mydei leaned back against the counter, trying to keep his voice steady even though his heart was beating faster than normal.

“I’ve been thinking about us since last night,” he started. “Actually, I’ve been thinking about it a lot today. This… whatever we’re doing.” He exhaled. “It’s obvious we both feel something. I like you, Phainon. More than just as a friend. And I’m pretty sure you feel the same.”

Phainon’s eyes met his. He didn’t deny it.

“I do,” he admitted quietly. “A lot.”

Mydei nodded, relieved but still careful.

“But… it’s still really soon. I moved here to rebuild my life, and you’ve got so much on your plate already. I don’t want to rush into something and make it complicated for either of us.” He gave a small, hesitant smile. “So I guess I just wanted to clarify where we stand. I’m not seeing anyone else. I don’t want to see anyone else. But I also don’t want to put pressure on you. We can keep taking it slow if that’s what you need.”

The kitchen fell quiet except for the gentle sizzling of vegetables behind them.

Phainon stepped closer until there was barely any space between them. His gaze dropped to Mydei’s lips for a moment before returning to his eyes.

“I don’t want anyone else either,” he said. “And slow sounds good. I’ve been scared I’d mess this up if I moved too fast.” A faint, crooked smile appeared. “But I really, really like having you here. In my messy little house. In my messy little life.”

Mydei felt something tickle in his chest. The tension didn’t disappear completely, but it changed from nervous uncertainty into something easier to stomach. Anticipation? Perhaps.

He reached out and lightly brushed a stray silver strand away from Phainon’s forehead.

“Then let’s keep doing this,” Mydei murmured.

Phainon leaned into the touch, eyes fluttering close for a second. When he opened them again, the smile on his face was soft and genuine.

“I can do that,” he whispered.

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Secret Cove
chapters.html:
They finally turned their attention back to the stove before the vegetables turned to mush. The simple meal came together quickly, and they carried their plates to the small table again. This time the silence between them felt comfortable instead of tense. Every so often their eyes would meet and they’d share a small, shy smile.

After dinner, they moved to the couch. Phainon poured them the last of the wine and put on some soft music in the background. The earlier tension had mostly melted away, replaced by a gentle awareness of each other.

To lighten the mood further, Phainon reached for an old photo album tucked on the bottom shelf.

“Alright, since you’re stuck with me figuring things out… fair warning,” he said with a playful grin. “I’m about to expose myself.”

He opened the album across their laps. Page after page revealed a much younger Phainon. There were photos of him covered in mud after chasing chickens, one of him proudly holding up a too-big fish, another where he was fast asleep on his grandmother’s lap with chocolate smeared on his face.

Mydei laughed openly, warm and delighted at each new picture.

“Oh my God, you were adorable,” he said, pointing at a photo of tiny Phainon trying to ride a too-big bicycle. “Look at those cheeks. Criminal.”

Phainon groaned, but he was smiling. “I was a menace.”

Mydei kept flipping pages, clearly enjoying himself. At one particularly cute photo, six year-old Phainon wearing a too-big sun hat and holding a lemon twice the size of his fist, made him pause.

“Can I take a picture of this one?” Mydei asked, already reaching for his phone. “This is too good to leave in the album.”

Phainon raised an eyebrow, leaning in closer. “What? The current me isn’t cute enough for you anymore?”

The teasing was light, but his voice had dropped a little. Their shoulders were pressed together, and Mydei suddenly became very aware of how close they were.

Mydei slowly lowered his phone, turning to look at Phainon properly.

“You’re more than cute now,” he murmured.

That perfectly stirred the peaceful atmosphere they were trying to create. Phainon’s eyes dropped to Mydei’s lips, then back up. Mydei’s heart pounded in his chest.

Slowly, Phainon lifted a hand and cupped the side of Mydei’s face, thumb brushing gently over his cheekbone. Mydei leaned into the touch.

Then they were kissing.

What started as soft press of lips became something more. The moment Mydei kissed him back, something in Phainon seemed to let go. His other hand found Mydei’s waist, pulling him closer on the couch. Mydei threaded his fingers through his hair, savoring the sound Phainon made against his mouth.

When they finally parted, they stayed close, breathing each other in.

Phainon let out a shaky little laugh. “Been wanting to do that for days.”

Mydei smiled, eyes still closed. “Took you long enough.”

They kissed again, slower this time, hands exploring with gentle curiosity.

---

The days that followed, Mydei caught himself smiling more often than not. He looked forward to going out now, something he never thought he’d say after moving here for peace and quiet. Every afternoon or evening, there was a good chance he’d run into Phainon, or Phainon would simply show up at his house with a new excuse to spend time together.

Their “slow” pace had evolved naturally. They still hadn’t put a label on it, but the affection was undeniable.

“You make the quiet feel good,” Phainon had told him two nights ago while they were sitting on the couch.

And Mydei had replied by kissing him deeper, because he felt exactly the same.

This particular morning, Mydei stood in front of the mirror adjusting his shirt before heading to the village. He had a tutoring session with Caelus in the afternoon, but he was already looking forward to the evening because Phainon had promised to take him to a hidden cove after his last delivery shift.

When he arrived at Mr. Kostas’s house, Caelus was already waiting at the table, earbuds out and notebook open. The edgy teenager demeanor hadn’t disappeared completely, but the hostility had softened considerably over the past week.

“Hey,” Caelus greeted him, almost casually.

Mydei raised an eyebrow, pleasantly surprised. “No sighing today? I’m honored.”

Caelus rolled his eyes, but there was a small smirk. “Yeah, yeah. Let’s just get this over with. I actually understood that reading passage you gave me last time, so maybe don’t make it too easy today.”

They spent the next hour going over conversation practice and vocabulary. Caelus was actually participating now. He argued in English about why his favorite football player was better than Mydei’s suggestion, and even cracked a joke in broken but improving sentences. By the end of the session, Mydei felt a genuine sense of progress.

“You’re getting better faster than you think,” Mydei told him as they wrapped up. “Keep this up and you’ll do fine in the city.”

Caelus shrugged, but his ears turned a little pink. “It’s not terrible having you as a teacher, I guess.”

High praise from a fourteen-year-old.

---

As Mydei walked back down toward the harbor later that evening, the sky was already soft pinks and oranges. He felt lighter. The tutoring was working out. His days had rhythm again. And best of all —

A familiar scooter pulled up beside him.

Phainon killed the engine and swung off, helmet under one arm. His hair was messy from the ride, and he was still wearing his delivery vest, but the moment he saw Mydei, his whole face softened.

“Hey, you,” Phainon said, stepping close without hesitation. He leaned in and pressed a quick, warm kiss to Mydei’s lips, right there on the side of the road like it was the most natural thing in the world. “Missed you.”

Mydei smiled against his mouth before pulling back. “It’s only been a day.”

“Exactly. Too long.” Phainon’s hand found Mydei’s waist, thumb brushing gently over his shirt. “How was the kid today?”

“Surprisingly cooperative. I think he’s starting to actually enjoy it a little.”

“See? Told you you’d be good at this.” Phainon’s voice dropped softer. “Proud of you.”

Mydei felt that familiar warmth in his chest again. He reached up and brushed a silver strand away from Phainon’s forehead, letting his fingers linger.

“Ready to show me this secret cove of yours?” he asked.

Phainon’s grin turned playful. He took Mydei’s hand without thinking, intertwining their fingers.

“But you have to let me kiss you as much as I want when we get there.”

Mydei squeezed his hand, heart feeling impossibly full.

“We have an agreement then.”

They walked together toward the scooter as the sun continued to set.

---

The scooter ride took them along a narrow, winding road that eventually turned into little more than a dirt path. When they finally stopped and he killed the engine, Mydei understood why this place was kept secret.

The secret cove was breathtaking.

A small, secluded beach nestled between steep cliffs covered in wild greenery. The water was clear with a gradient of turquoise and deep sapphire that glowed even in the fading evening light. Smooth white pebbles lined the shore instead of sand, and a few ancient olive trees clung to the rocks above.

Mydei stood frozen at the edge of the path, bag slipping from his shoulder.

“Phainon…” he breathed. “This is… incredible.”

He’d visited a few famous tourist spots and scenic nature reserves before, but nothing had ever felt quite like this. This place was untouched. Like the coast itself had decided to hide its most beautiful secret away from the world.

Phainon came up behind him, wrapping his arms around Mydei’s waist and resting his chin on his shoulder.

“So… do you like it?” he asked softly, a hint of nervousness in his voice.

Mydei turned in his arms, eyes shining. Instead of answering with words, he cupped Phainon’s face with both hands and kissed him.

It was deep, grateful, and full of the warmth that had been building between them for days. Phainon made a surprised but pleased sound against his lips before kissing him back just as eagerly, hands sliding up Mydei’s back to pull him closer.

When they broke apart for air, Mydei didn’t go far. He pressed another kiss to the corner of Phainon’s mouth, then his jaw, then the sensitive spot just below his ear.

“I love it,” he murmured between kisses. “Thank you for bringing me here.”

Phainon’s laugh was a little breathless. “If this is the reaction I get, I should’ve brought you sooner.”

Mydei pulled back just enough to look at him properly. The sunset painted Phainon’s face in warm oranges and pinks, catching beautifully in the silver streaks of his hair. His eyes were soft, almost wondering.

“You keep showing me pieces of this place I never knew existed,” Mydei said quietly. “The market, your apartment, now this cove… It feels like you’re sharing your whole world with me.”

Phainon’s expression turned serious for a moment. He brushed his thumb across Mydei’s cheek.

“Because I want to,” he said simply. “I want you in it.”

They kissed again, slower this time, savoring the taste of salt air and each other. The waves crashed against the pebbles as the sky slowly turned deep indigo above them. When they finally pulled apart, Phainon took Mydei’s hand and led him down to the smooth pebbles, where they sat together, watching the last light disappear over the water.

Mydei leaned his head against Phainon’s shoulder, heart full in a way he hadn’t known was possible.

This quiet life he had run toward… was starting to feel like home.

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Boyfriend-like
chapters.html:
One evening a few days later, Mydei walked up the familiar path to Phainon’s small apartment with a bottle of local wine and some fresh figs he’d picked up at the market. He didn’t knock and simply pushed the door open with a soft, “Hey, it’s me.”

He was greeted by a startled yelp.

Phainon stood in the middle of the living room in an old black tank top and shorts, plastic gloves on his hands, and half his hair covered in thick gray dye. The other half was still his natural dark with silver streaks. He looked like a startled raccoon caught mid-heist.

“Shit—! You’re early,” Phainon laughed, embarrassed. “I thought I’d be done before you came over.”

Mydei blinked, then broke into a smile. “You’re dyeing your hair gray? On purpose?”

Phainon rubbed the back of his neck, smearing a bit of dye there. “It’s low-maintenance. The silver was already coming in strong anyway, so I figured I’d just lean into it. Makes the whole ‘tired delivery boy’ look intentional.”

Mydei set the wine and figs down and stepped closer, amused. “You need help?”

Phainon hesitated for half a second, then gave him that slightly shy smile. “Yeah… I’d actually really like that.”

They moved into the tiny bathroom. Phainon sat on a wooden stool while Mydei stood in front of him. The space was so small that Mydei’s body was practically between Phainon’s knees. He pulled on the spare pair of gloves Phainon handed him and carefully started working the dye through the untreated sections of hair.

“You know,” Mydei said, gently massaging the dye in with his fingertips, “most people your age try to hide the gray. You’re running toward it.”

Phainon chuckled. “I’ve been working three jobs and stressing about money since I was twenty-two. Might as well look like I’ve lived a little.” He tilted his head obediently as Mydei worked. “Besides, I think it looks good. What do you think?”

Mydei smiled softly, focused on a stubborn strand near Phainon’s temple. “I think you’ll look unfairly hot with full gray hair. It already suits you.”

The compliment made Phainon go quiet. He was trying to focus on their conversation, but he kept getting distracted. Mydei was so close.

Standing right in front of him, gentle hands in his hair, the soft scent of his soap mixed with the chemical smell of dye, that focused little expression on his face. Every time Mydei leaned in to reach the back of his head, his shirt rode up slightly and Phainon’s hands itched to touch.

Eventually, Phainon couldn’t resist anymore.

While Mydei was carefully coating a section near his forehead, Phainon slowly slid both hands around Mydei’s waist. He didn’t pull him closer and simply held him there, fingers gently squeezing the warm skin under the hem of Mydei’s shirt. His thumbs brushed against Mydei’s sides.

Mydei’s hands stilled for a moment.

“…Distracted?” he asked, voice slightly amused but noticeably softer.

“Very,” Phainon admitted, looking up at him. “You’re standing between my legs looking all focused and boyfriend-like. It’s unfair.”

Mydei’s breath caught at the word boyfriend, but he didn’t correct him. Instead, he leaned down and pressed a lingering kiss to Phainon’s lips, careful not to get dye anywhere.

Phainon squeezed his waist a little tighter, kissing him back with hunger. When they parted, Mydei booped his nose playfully.

“Behave until I finish your hair,” he whispered. “Then you can be as distracted as you want.”

Phainon let out a sigh, hands still firmly on Mydei’s waist.

“Yes, sir.”

Mydei continued working the dye through Phainon’s hair, while Phainon kept holding him close like he never wanted to let go.

---

After the dye had set and been rinsed out, Phainon sat on the stool again while Mydei dried his hair. The new gray looked striking, cooler and more intentional than the scattered silver streaks before. It suited him perfectly, sharpening his already handsome features.

“You’re spoiling me,” Phainon murmured, eyes half-closed in satisfaction as Mydei’s fingers worked through his damp hair.

“You deserve a little spoiling,” Mydei replied softly. “Hold still. I’m going to trim the ends a bit. They’re getting uneven.”

He picked up the small pair of scissors Phainon had set out and carefully snipped away the split ends, shaping the hair around his face and neck. Phainon stayed still, hands resting on Mydei’s hips again, occasionally squeezing whenever Mydei leaned in close.

When Mydei finally stepped back to admire his work, Phainon looked up at him with a lazy, fond smile.

“Damn. I look good.”

“You do,” Mydei agreed, running his fingers through the fresh gray hair one last time. “Very distinguished. Dangerously attractive.”

Phainon chuckled and pulled Mydei down into a slow kiss, tasting a little bit of toothpaste.

“I’m going to visit my grandma tomorrow afternoon,” he said quietly. “I usually try to go once or twice a week. Bring her some groceries, help with things around the apartment, listen to her scold me for working too much…” He hesitated, thumbs brushing on Mydei’s waist. “Would you want to come with me? No pressure if it feels too soon. She’s a little nosy and very opinionated, but she’s important to me.”

Mydei’s heart gave a small, nervous flutter. Meeting Phainon’s grandmother felt like a significant step. But looking down at Phainon’s hopeful expression, Mydei found his answer easily.

“I want to meet her.”

Phainon’s face lit up with genuine relief and joy. He stood up from the stool, wrapping Mydei in a full hug, face buried in his neck.

“Yeah?” he whispered against his skin. “She’s going to love you. Probably try to feed you until you explode. And she’ll definitely interrogate you about your intentions with her favorite grandson.”

Mydei laughed softly, hugging him back just as tightly. “I’ll prepare my answers in advance.”

Phainon eventually pulled back just enough to look at him, eyes soft.

“Thanks a lot for today,” he said sincerely.

Mydei brushed a stray gray strand away from Phainon’s forehead and smiled.

“Anytime.”

---

The next afternoon, they rode Phainon’s scooter out past the village, following the coastal road for a while before turning inland. The apartment complex was modest but well-kept. A cluster of small buildings surrounded by flowering bushes and shaded walkways, located just a short distance from the local hospital. It was clearly a neighborhood favored by elderly residents as many sat on balconies or benches, watching the world go by.

The moment they parked and Phainon took off his helmet, the greetings began.

“Phainon! My favorite delivery boy!” an old woman with a walking cane called out, smiling brightly.

Another man playing cards under a tree waved. “Eh, look who finally remembered he has a grandmother!”

Phainon laughed easily, falling into his usual charming self.
